legend.check_optimizations_for: per scope and kernel, the range of the named dim it also runs at (checked at every size there), why others do not, and whole-model timings at the recorded serve sizes
legend.target_workload: the workload nominated before timing; its whole-model win must repeat before installation
legend.timing_case: the captured input case behind this hypothesis's local kernel timings
legend.timing_workload: the workload behind a region's recorded shipped-kernel speedup
legend.model_ratios: per-workload products of incremental model ratios; diagnostic estimates, not final measurements
legend.p: share of one step this region costs, all copies together, per workload
legend.T_orig_ms: library time for all copies, per workload, from pricing
legend.T_rep_ms: library time for one copy, per workload, from pricing
legend.roofline_ms: estimated ideal cost of one copy from boundary traffic and arithmetic
legend.s_max: optimistic headroom estimate: library time divided by estimated ideal cost
legend.bound: estimated limiting resource: memory, known compute, or launch; custom arithmetic may be unknown
legend.s: speedup shipped: the library's time over the shipped kernel's, both from the kernel's own ship clock
legend.region_ms: the kernel's time for one pass of one copy, from the ship clock
legend.library_ms: the library's time for the same pass, measured beside it
legend.win_ms: library_ms minus region_ms; positive means the kernel is faster
legend.sigma_ms: uncertainty of win_ms; a ship needs a win past three of these
legend.stranded: regions dropped before the search, grouped by reason
legend.steps_per_sample: dependent model steps in one timed sample of the step clock; more than one when a step is too short to bring the GPU clock up on its own
legend.min_win_ms: the least a region win had to save per step on this workload: 1% of the step, at most constants.min_win_ms; the three-sigma rule decides the rest
legend.speedup_vs_plain: under the compiled baseline: the finished model against plain eager MLX, paired in one window at the end of the job; compile's own gain is included, since the model runs compiled
legend.speedup_vs_compiled: under the plain baseline: the finished model (eager plus its kernels) against the untouched model under mx.compile, measured the same way; under 1 means compile alone is faster
legend.plain_win_confirmed: whether that comparison resolved a win past three sigma (compiled_win_confirmed likewise)
legend.plain_loss_confirmed: whether it resolved a loss (compiled_loss_confirmed likewise)
legend.measured_compute_gflops: the plain-matmul rate per dtype clocked in the region's own pricing window; the compute term of its estimated limit divides the region's flops by it
legend.close_rule: why a region's search ended: its budget or the job's is spent, the operator asked to finish, or no discernible headroom (launch-bound, head unmoved by the last two attempts, the last three kernels each within one sigma of the launch floor clocked beside them)
legend.constants.openers_per_region: how many attempts a region's widening round holds at most, each an opener written against the scaffold from a different agent-generated direction; limited by the remaining attempt budget
legend.delivery: how a kernel installs at the region's scope, per workload: direct, graph (the scope compiled with the cut inserted) or replay
legend.library_arm: what the region's clocks ran the library as, per workload: plain ops, or one compiled graph where graph delivery compiles the scope
legend.baseline.clocks_ms.compiled: under library inference: the model with its outermost compilable scopes compiled and empty, the baseline unless the manifest asks for plain
legend.final.delivery: under a plain baseline: the untouched model against the installed scopes compiled with no kernel, and that against the patched model

hypotheses.hypothesis: Three launches. (1) Each row gets layer_norm, then the bf16 (1+shift) multiply and add, rounded after every op like the original. (2) A tiled 4-bit affine qmm uses 64x64 output tiles, BK=32 and 4 simdgroups (2x2, each 32x32 as 4x4 float 8x8 fragments). It dequantizes W into threadgroup float and loads A from the stage-1 bf16. The epilogue routes each 64-column tile: MLP columns go to out0, V columns go straight to out1 transposed, and Q/K go to a 2816x6144 scratch. (3) One simdgroup per (token, head) does the float rms_norm, the bf16 round trip, RoPE and a transposed store. Benefit: removes the split/transpose/astype/stack traffic, about 150MB per copy. The matmul changes accumulation order, so this is tagged changing. It is the correct baseline for the other designs.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: Keep the stage split, but the qmm stores A and dequantized W in threadgroup as bfloat and multiplies bfloat simdgroup matrices into float accumulators. Tiles grow to 64x128 with 8 simdgroups. Halving threadgroup bytes and using bf16 MMA throughput (3295 vs 2780 GFLOPS) targets the compute bound. This differs from h1 in fragment dtype and tile shape, not just size.
hypotheses.summary: shipped: whole-model correctness and independent timing confirmation passed

hypotheses.hypothesis: Drop the normalized-activation buffer. A tiny stats stage writes per-row mean and inverse std. The qmm A-loader then applies layer_norm and modulation, with the same bf16 roundings, while it reads raw in0. This saves one 17MB write and read plus a launch, and moves elementwise work into load latency. It differs from h1 in where the prologue math lives.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Double-buffer threadgroup tiles. Each thread fetches the next K-slab of A and the packed W words into registers while the simdgroups multiply the current slab, with one barrier per step. This hides global and dequant latency behind MMA, a scheduling change distinct from h1's serial load-then-compute loop.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Each 128-wide N tile of the q and k region is exactly one head. The qmm epilogue can do the per-row rms_norm and RoPE from the staged float tile and write out2 and out3 directly. This removes the 35MB tmp1 round trip and one launch, with the same bf16 rounding points as context_1.

hypotheses.hypothesis: h6 failed to compile because thread_elements() does not return a 2-vector under this header. Replace it with simdgroup_store into a small float staging area. The staging covers 16 rows x 128 columns, stride 132, and takes 4 passes. After each pass all threads convert the staged floats to a bfloat Cs tile of 64x136. Total threadgroup memory is about 25.9KB, with staging and Cs placed after the As and Bs use ends. The RMS and RoPE epilogue then reads Cs as h6 intended. This removes the tmp1 round trip (about 35MB of write plus read) and the third launch. Values and rounding points are unchanged from h2, so expect a few ms saved.

hypotheses.hypothesis: In the h2-style qmm, the A-slab loader reads 8 scalar bf16 per thread; replace it with one 16-byte vector load. Replace the per-element scale and bias dequant writes with packed bfloat4 threadgroup stores. This cuts loader instruction count, which competes with MMA issue in a compute-bound loop.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Grow the h2 or h7 K-slab from 32 to 64 so it matches the quantization group. Each slab then needs one scale and bias load per row and half as many barrier pairs. Threadgroup memory rises only to about 27KB, which is less than h4's double buffer. The goal is to cut loop and barrier overhead in the compute-bound qmm.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Remap the linear threadgroup id so that groups of 8 M-tiles walk the same N-tiles together. The packed W columns and their scales then stay cache-resident across the M-tiles that consume them, instead of the whole 42MB weight streaming once per M-tile row. This reorders the schedule only, not the math. It can be combined with whichever of h7 and h8 is faster.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Keep the 2-pass staging but have each thread convert 8 consecutive floats and write one 16-byte packed bf16 store to out0, out1 or tmp1. The destination is known per tile, so the branch can be hoisted. This cuts the 16 scalar stores per thread per pass without adding threadgroup memory.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Keep h10's qmm unchanged, including its tile footprint, vectorized epilogue and math. Change only the raster swizzle group from 4 M-tiles to 11 M-tiles; 11 divides the 44 M-tiles exactly. Threadgroups running at the same time then share about 2-3 N-tiles of dequantized weight columns across 11 activation row-tiles, instead of about 6 N-tiles across 4. Each 196KB packed-W tile and its scales should be reused more while hot in cache. The resident A set (11 x 393KB, about 4.3MB) should still fit the system cache. This follows lesson 7: schedule-only changes that leave the footprint alone have been the safe lever. Expected gain is a fraction of a millisecond toward the roofline.

hypotheses.hypothesis: h11 widened h10's swizzle group from 4 to 11 M-tiles and lost 1.09 ms, so the optimum may sit at or below 4. Keep h10 exactly: same qmm tile footprint, the same 16-byte vectorized epilogue, the same norm and rope stages. Change only GM from 4 to 2, which divides the 44 M-tiles. Concurrent threadgroups then span more N-tiles with fewer activation rows, so the resident A set shrinks to about 0.8MB and the working set of dequantized W columns grows. This tests the other side of the GM curve. A gain would be a fraction of a millisecond on the 0.8 ms gap to the roofline.

hypotheses.hypothesis: One dispatch does the whole chain. Each 64x64 output tile gets 4 SIMD groups, and each group owns a 32x32 block of 4x4 float 8x8 simdgroup_matrix accumulators. Per K-slab of 16, the loader builds the A slab on the fly: it reads in2 directly for k<3072, and otherwise computes bf16(in0*in1), rounding exactly like the recorded mul. It also dequantizes one packed uint32 of W per thread with its group scale and bias into float threadgroup tiles of about 10KB. The epilogue applies the recorded bf16 roundings of qmm, then *in6, then +in7. Expected benefit: the 9216-wide product and the 12288-wide concat, about 70MB each, never reach memory, and the scale/add epilogue is fused. This is the baseline fused design.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: Two stages. Stage 1 is a vectorized elementwise pass that writes the bf16 concat [M,12288] once. Stage 2 is a qmm whose A loader is a pure 16-byte vector copy with no branch or multiply, and whose epilogue is fused. This differs from h1 by trading one extra ~70MB write+read for a simpler hot loader. It tests whether loader ALU work in the compute-bound loop costs more than the traffic.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: Stage 1 dequantizes W once into bf16 [3072,12288]. Stage 2 is a plain bf16 GEMM with the A fusion and epilogue. This removes the per-tile dequant, which h1 repeats 44 times per weight element, at the cost of a 75MB write and read. It is a different amortization of weight work from h1 and h2.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: A 256-thread threadgroup covers 128x64 with 8 SIMD groups, and the B tile is dequantized once per 128 rows instead of 64. That halves dequant and weight reads per flop compared with h1, using a bf16 threadgroup tile to keep the footprint under about 16KB. This tests a larger reuse block rather than staging.

hypotheses.kind: deeper slab with K-major weight tile
hypotheses.hypothesis: Starting from h1/h4 (64x64 tile, 4 SIMD groups, each owning 32x32 of float 8x8 accumulators, with register prefetch of the next slab as in h4), BK goes from 16 to 32. That doubles the MMA steps between barrier pairs, from 2 to 4, which matches the library qmm's slab depth. The dequantized W tile is now stored K-major as Bs[k][n], so every w fragment uses a plain simdgroup_load instead of the transposed load both slow kernels used. A is loaded with two 16-byte vector reads per operand and written as 16 contiguous floats. The footprint is about 18KB: As is 64x36 floats and Bs is 32x68. Expected: fewer barriers, no transposed fragment loads and wide global loads cut h1's 350 ms substantially. If this barely moves, the bottleneck lies elsewhere, such as dequant cost or the epilogue.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: Every fused kernel runs about 5x behind the library, and h5 added code and got slower. That pattern fits the 4x4 simdgroup_matrix accumulator array, plus the a and w fragment arrays, being indexed from loops the compiler did not fully unroll. The arrays would then sit in spilled thread-local stack memory instead of registers, and every MMA would pay memory round trips. The change keeps h1's kernel exactly and adds '#pragma clang loop unroll(full)' to every loop that indexes acc, a, w or the fragment elements, including the init, MMA, load and epilogue loops, as MLX steel does with STEEL_PRAGMA_UNROLL. The math and the order of operations are unchanged. If spills were the cause, the time should drop sharply toward the library's 77 ms. If it barely moves, spilling is ruled out and the per-slab load, dequant and barrier structure becomes the suspect.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.kind: deeper pipelined slab on unrolled tile
hypotheses.hypothesis: h6 is 81.6 ms against the library's 76.8. Its loop runs only 2 MMA k-steps per barrier pair, its global loads are scalar, and each load stalls before its own slab's MMA. Keeping h6's fully unrolled 64x64 tile and 4 SIMD groups, this change raises BK to 32, so 4 MMA steps sit between each barrier pair and there are half as many barriers. Loads become 16-byte uint4 loads of raw bf16, and the next slab is prefetched into registers (raw A words, two packed weight words, scale and bias) while the current slab's MMAs run. The rounding points match h6: the in0*in1 product rounds to bf16, and dequantized weights round to bf16 before the float MMA. The expected effect is hidden load latency and fewer barriers, bringing the kernel under the library time.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: Remap threadgroup ids so that groups of 4 M-tiles walk N-tiles together. Weight tiles and A rows then stay cache-resident across neighbouring threadgroups, which was a schedule-only win in the other qmm region (lesson_7). The tile footprint is unchanged.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: Keep the winner of h5/h1. Stage the 32x32 accumulator block through threadgroup memory so that each thread applies *in6 and +in7 with the recorded bf16 roundings and writes 16-byte packed bf16 rows instead of scalar 2-byte stores. This cuts uncoalesced epilogue traffic for the in7 reads and out0 writes.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: On the h7 tile with BK 16 per buffer, keep two threadgroup buffers so the register-prefetched slab is written into the idle buffer while MMAs read the other. This removes one of the two barriers per slab and hides the threadgroup write behind the MMAs. Memory fits under 32 KB.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: Apply lesson_14's full unrolling to a 64x128 tile with 8 SIMD groups, each owning 32x32, using the better of h7 and h8 as the slab pipeline. Each A slab, including the in0*in1 product and its bf16 rounding, is then built once per 128 output columns instead of 64. That halves A reads from global memory and halves the A conversion ALU per flop, which targets the roughly 2.5 ms gap to the library.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: h9 ties the library (win 0.006 ms, sigma 0.08). Its float threadgroup slabs take 192*36*4 = 27.6 KB, which likely allows only one resident threadgroup per core and leaves barrier and load latency exposed. Every staged value is already bf16-exact: the A copies, the in0*in1 product rounded to bf16, and the dequantized weights rounded to bf16. The change is to store the slabs as bfloat16_t with LD = 40, which halves them to 15 KB inside one 16 KB buffer that the float epilogue reuses. A slabs become single 16-byte copies and B slabs become two 16-byte packed stores. Fragments are filled per lane with thread_elements(), using the standard 8x8 lane coordinate map (fm, fn), and converted to float for the unchanged float MMA and epilogue. Expected effect: two threadgroups per core and fewer threadgroup store instructions, which should give a measurable win over the library.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Online-softmax flash attention built on simdgroup_float8x8 fragments. Each 128-thread threadgroup owns 32 query rows of one head, one SIMD group per 8 rows. Q is prescaled by scale*log2e and held in 16 register fragments. 16-key tiles of K and V are staged into threadgroup memory as float. QK^T uses transposed fragment loads. The row max and sum are computed per tile by 4 lanes per row with shuffles, the O rows are rescaled by a diagonal fragment multiply, and the P*V products accumulate into 16 O fragments. The O rows are normalized once at the end. This avoids materializing the 2816x2816 score matrix. It is a correct baseline for the tensor-core path, and I expect it near but probably slower than the MLX steel kernel because of the diagonal rescale overhead and small key tiles.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: Same flash structure, but the scores and O stay in registers. The fragment elements are addressed through thread_elements() with the known 8x8 lane layout, so the row max, sum and rescale happen in registers with no threadgroup round trip for S and no diagonal multiplies. K and V tiles stay as bf16 in threadgroup memory with 32-key tiles, halving the barriers. This differs from o1 by removing the S staging and the rescale matmuls, which are o1's main overhead.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: No simdgroup matrices. Each thread owns one query row: 128 floats of Q scaled in registers plus a 128-float O accumulator. The threads stream shared K and V tiles from threadgroup memory with an FMA loop and per-key online softmax. This tests whether plain FMA throughput and simple code can compete, and it differs completely from the fragment designs in its data layout and compute unit use.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: Two stages. Stage 1 splits the key axis into 4 chunks. Each chunk runs the o1-style flash tile loop and writes partial unnormalized O, the row max m and the row sum l to scratch. Stage 2 merges the chunks per row with log-sum-exp weights and writes bf16. This gives shorter per-threadgroup loops and more concurrent threadgroups for better core balance, at the cost of extra scratch traffic. It differs from the others by decomposing along the keys.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Edit of head o3_scalarrow. At staging time each thread converts its bf16 chunk of K and V to float once and stores it in threadgroup memory: 16-key float tiles with row pitch 132. The inner QK and PV loops then read float4s and issue pure FMAs, with no per-element shift or mask. Per thread, this removes about 64 integer ops out of roughly 132 per key. Each thread's dims are interleaved (d = t*16 + sub*4 + e), so the 4 sub-lanes read consecutive float4s without bank conflicts. BK=16 also halves the s[] registers. Expected: a clear drop from 103 ms if ALU unpack is the bottleneck. The cost is twice as many barriers per key.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Each group of 8 lanes owns 2 query rows, and each lane covers 16 dims of both rows. Every threadgroup float4 read of K/V then feeds 2 rows' FMAs, which halves threadgroup load traffic per FMA. Each threadgroup covers 128 query rows, which halves the device K/V reloads across query blocks.

hypotheses.kind: steel-style simdgroup with float K/V and transposed load
hypotheses.hypothesis: Revisit the simdgroup family with the MLX steel layout. There are 64 query rows per threadgroup with 8 simdgroups, and each simdgroup owns 8 rows. K is loaded as a transposed fragment via simdgroup_load(..., transpose) from a float tile. The softmax runs on thread_elements in registers, and the pre-converted float tiles are shared by all 8 simdgroups. This tests whether matrix units win once staging is amortized over 64 rows.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.kind: bf16 threadgroup tiles, K pre-transposed, 32-key blocks
hypotheses.hypothesis: This edits h7_sgsteel, which is currently head at 36.9 ms against the library's 33.5 ms. Three changes. First, K and V stay bf16 in threadgroup memory, which halves the threadgroup bytes staged and read per key (lesson 23 found float staging costly). Second, K is stored transposed as Kt[d][key] with pitch 40, so each lane builds its K^T fragment with one 32-bit word read. V fragments are also one word read per lane with pitch 136. Both pitches are chosen to be bank-conflict free, and the bf16 values are expanded to float by bit shifts, as in MLX steel. Third, BK rises from 16 to 32, which fits because the tiles are about 19 KB. That halves barriers and loop overhead per key and gives 4 score fragments per softmax step. The expected result is reduced threadgroup traffic and synchronization, enough to close the roughly 3.4 ms gap to the library. The math is unchanged except that the accumulation grouping now spans 32-key blocks.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: This edits h7_sgsteel (head, 36.9 ms against the library's 33.5 ms) and keeps its float tiles, simdgroup_load fragments and math. The one change is software pipelining. Each thread holds its uint4 chunks of K and V for the next 16-key block in registers. It issues those global loads immediately after the staging barrier, before the current block's QK, softmax and PV matrix work, and writes them to threadgroup memory only at the top of the next iteration. Heavy fragment register use likely limits occupancy, so global-load latency is probably exposed between the two barriers in h7. Overlapping it with the 64 MMAs per block should cut part of the roughly 10% gap. Threadgroup memory and register cost stay about the same (8 more uints per thread).
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: h9's register prefetch lost to h7 (37.6 vs 36.9 ms), so this starts from h7 instead. When kb+16 <= Lk (every block for Lk=2816), the kernel takes a uniform branch that skips all per-element validity compares and selects. In the tail block, masked scores are set to -1e30 and exp2 naturally yields 0, which removes the four p selects. This trims ALU work in the softmax step between the MMAs.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: Use the MLX-like steel config: 32 query rows per threadgroup and 4 simdgroups (128 threads), with float K/V tiles. Each threadgroup is smaller, so each core holds more of them, which hides barrier stalls. The cost is twice the staging per query row.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Stage A is one launch that runs all four 4-bit qmms as a flat tile list: 64x64 tiles, BK=32, four simdgroups each owning a 32x32 block of float 8x8 MMAs, and about 17.9KB of threadgroup memory. Weights are dequantized on the fly into float threadgroup tiles. V results go straight into out0 in [h, s, d] layout, which removes the transposes and the concat. The added q and k results go to bf16 scratch. Stage B uses one simdgroup per (head, token) row. It reads the in4/in5 rows or the scratch rows, then applies rms_norm, rounds to bf16, applies RoPE and writes out1/out2. Expected result: well under the library's 41 ms, because the 4 qmm launches, 4 norms, concats and the float round trips become 2 launches.

hypotheses.kind: bf16 threadgroup tiles with vector loaders and swizzle
hypotheses.hypothesis: Stage A replaces h1's qmm loaders and keeps its 4-job flat tile list, 64x64 tile, BK=32 and float 8x8 accumulators. A is held in threadgroup memory as bf16 and filled with two 16-byte vector loads per thread, instead of 16 scalar float stores. W is dequantized word by word, with the same bf16 rounding as h1, and stored n-major as one 16-byte packed write per word, which removes h1's 8 strided scalar writes. MMA fragments are filled from bf16 using the MLX lane-coordinate map, and B is read transposed. Threadgroup memory drops to 10KB. The epilogue runs in two 32-row passes and writes 32-byte packed stores. Tiles are rasterized in groups of 4 M-tiles sharing N-tiles (the GM=4 result from region 5bc62). Stage B is unchanged. Expected effect: h1's 137 ms comes mostly from loader instruction count and footprint, so this should cut it several-fold toward the library's 39.5 ms. It differs from h1 in data layout and loaders, not in the math.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: The qmm uses BN=128 so that each tile covers exactly one head. The added q and k tiles then do rms_norm and RoPE in the epilogue from the staged C tile and write out1/out2 directly, with no scratch round trip. The main q and k norm+rope is a separate lightweight stage that can overlap. This differs from h1 by removing the tmp buffers and fusing across the qmm boundary; it risks the occupancy cost that lesson_4 warns about.
hypotheses.summary: shipped: whole-model correctness and independent timing confirmation passed

hypotheses.hypothesis: Keep h2's schedule, math and 15KB tile footprint unchanged: one launch, BN=128 head-wide 64x128 tiles, BK=32, GM=4 swizzle and the fused norm+RoPE epilogue. Change only when the global loads are issued. Right after the first barrier, before the current slab's MMAs, load the next K-slab's A uint4, its two packed weight words as one uint2, and its scale and bias into registers. Their latency then hides under the 64 MMAs per simdgroup. h2 stalls on every global load before each barrier. The dequant and accumulation order stay identical to h2. This differs from h1, h4b and h2 because it targets memory-latency hiding, not tile shape, loader width or fusion.

hypotheses.kind: taller M tile to halve dequant per output
hypotheses.hypothesis: Start from h5's prefetch pipeline and raise BM from 64 to 128, keeping BN=128 as one head. Each of the 8 simdgroups then owns a 32x64 block, which is acc[4][8]. Each dequantized weight slab is reused by twice as many rows, so dequant ALU work, weight/scale/bias fetches and barriers per output fall by half. The cost is a 20KB threadgroup footprint, 2x accumulator registers, and 720 threadgroups instead of 1440. The fused norm+RoPE epilogue and the rope-only tiles are unchanged, and the K accumulation order is unchanged. This tests whether the remaining ~1.5 ms gap comes from redundant dequant rather than memory latency. The single launch already overlaps all four jobs, so the split-launch h3 was dropped.

hypotheses.kind: deeper K slab aligned to quant group
hypotheses.hypothesis: Start from h5 (head at 24.97 ms) and keep its 64x128 head-wide tile, acc[4][4], GM=4 swizzle, register prefetch and fused norm+RoPE epilogue. Raise BK from 32 to 64 so each slab matches one quant group. The loop then runs 48 iterations instead of 96, halving the barriers. Each thread loads one uint4 of weight words, its scale and bias, and two uint4 of A per slab, so there are fewer and wider global loads. Per-thread accumulator registers stay the same, avoiding what I suspect was h6's spill. The kk order along K is unchanged. The risk is the footprint: 27.6KB lowers threadgroups per core.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: slower than the installed kernel in a fresh region comparison; model timing skipped

hypotheses.hypothesis: On the best qmm parent, replace the scalar bf16 and float loads in the rope-only tiles and the added-job epilogue with uint2 and float2 vector loads, cutting load instructions in the memory-side portion that overlaps the MMA tiles.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: whole-model speedup unresolved

hypotheses.hypothesis: Start from the best qmm parent (h5 or h8) and cut the dequant ALU per slab. Each thread converts its two packed words by extracting nibble pairs with a shift and mask on the whole word, then converting them together. The scale*q+bias math stays in float, so the values are unchanged. This tests whether the dequant ALU, not latency, is the remaining 1.5 ms gap to the roofline. It keeps the 64x128/BK=32 tile, acc[4][4] and the 15KB footprint, because h6 and h7 showed that bigger tiles or footprints lose.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: whole-model speedup unresolved

hypotheses.hypothesis: Starting from the best parent, drop the threadgroup A tile. Each simdgroup loads its 4 A 8x8 bf16 fragments with simdgroup_load straight from device memory; rows past M are clamped and their outputs are never stored. Only the dequantized B tile stays in threadgroup memory, which cuts the footprint from about 15KB to about 10KB for higher occupancy and removes the A store and bank traffic. This tests occupancy and loader cost rather than dequant ALU.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: slower than the installed kernel in a fresh region comparison; model timing skipped

hypotheses.kind: interleaved tile order mixing memory and MMA work
hypotheses.hypothesis: Keep h8's code as is: same qmm tiles, prefetch and epilogue. Change only the threadgroup-to-work mapping. h8 puts all 864 memory-bound norm+RoPE tiles after the 1440 compute-bound MMA tiles, so they run as a memory-bound tail after the MMA work. A Bresenham bijection spreads them evenly through the grid, about 3 rope tiles per 5 MMA tiles. Each core then holds a mix, and the rope tiles' streaming can hide under the MMA tiles' ALU work. The GM swizzle among MMA tiles is kept because the MMA index stays contiguous.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: whole-model speedup unresolved

hypotheses.hypothesis: On the best parent, double-buffer the A and B slabs so the register prefetch for slab k+1 is written to the other buffer. That leaves one barrier per K step. It is a footprint risk of about 30KB, per lesson_34.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: slower than the installed kernel in a fresh region comparison; model timing skipped

hypotheses.kind: wider M-group rasterization for cache reuse
hypotheses.hypothesis: Keep h8's code, math, 15KB footprint and epilogue unchanged. Change only the tile rasterization group GM from 4 to 8 M-tiles per head sweep. More concurrently resident tiles then share each head's packed weight words, scales and biases in the system cache, which cuts main-loop device load latency. h9, h12 and h13 point to that latency as the remaining gap. The change adds no registers or threadgroup memory, so the occupancy risk from lesson_33 and lesson_34 does not apply.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: whole-model speedup unresolved

hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: Reuse the library qmm_t_impl with BM=BN=64 and BK=32. The 2x2 simdgroups each own a 32x32 sub-tile instead of 16x16, so each threadgroup does four times the MMA work per barrier pair. Every staged X row and dequantized W row is reused twice as often, which halves loader and dequant work per flop and shared-memory traffic per MMA. Threadgroup memory is about 10KB, within the ~15KB comfort zone in earlier lessons. Each output is still accumulated in the same k order through the same fragment MMAs, so results stay bit-exact. This opener tests whether the kernel is limited by loads and dequant relative to MMA.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: whole-model speedup unresolved

hypotheses.hypothesis: Keep the scaffold's 32x32x32 tile math but remap threadgroup_position_in_grid so consecutive threadgroups sweep a narrow band of N-columns across many M-rows (grouped or swizzled order). With N=18432 and M=2304, the default raster walks all 576 column tiles per row band, so W (28MB packed plus scales) streams repeatedly. A column-band swizzle keeps the W slab and its scales resident in the system cache while X tiles cycle. This changes only scheduling order, never arithmetic, unlike h1 which changes the tile shape.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: Two stages. Stage 1 dequantizes W to a bf16 [N,K] scratch using the same scale*q+bias expression as QuantizedBlockLoader, which costs about 2ms of bandwidth. Stage 2 runs a dense transposed-B bf16 tiled MMA without per-tile dequant ALU. This removes the dequant work that the scaffold repeats for every one of the 72 M-tiles. Unlike h1 and h2, it moves dequant out of the compute-bound loop entirely.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: whole-model win did not repeat in independent confirmation

hypotheses.hypothesis: Keep BM=BN=32 but set BK=64, which equals the group size, so each W row slab uses exactly one scale/bias pair per load. This halves the barrier count per output and gives wider vector loads, at about 10KB of threadgroup memory. It tests barrier and loop overhead rather than reuse (h1), cache order (h2) or dequant placement (h3). The k order is unchanged.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: region did not nominate an installable replacement

hypotheses.hypothesis: Keep h3's dequant prepass and its 64x64x32 steel MMA with the same k order, so the result stays bit-exact. Remap threadgroup ids MLX-style with swizzle_log=3: eight consecutive threadgroups share one N-tile across a band of eight M-tiles, then the band sweeps N. With the plain raster, every M-tile row re-streams the whole 113MB bf16 W scratch, about 36 passes and roughly 4GB of traffic. The swizzle cuts that to about 5 passes, while the 3MB X band stays cache resident. Expected: the dense stage stops competing for DRAM and moves from about 75ms toward the pure-MMA time. Out-of-range M-tiles in the last band return before any barrier.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: whole-model speedup unresolved

hypotheses.hypothesis: Start from h5 and set BK=16 in stage 2, which is MLX's large-GEMM config. This cuts threadgroup memory from about 10KB to about 6KB so more threadgroups are resident per core, which hides load latency behind MMA. The k order is unchanged, so the result stays exact.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Start from h5 and use a 64x128 output tile with WM=2, WN=4 (8 simdgroups). Each X slab is then reused across twice the columns, which halves X threadgroup loads per flop. The k order is unchanged.

hypotheses.kind: taller M tile, bigger per-simdgroup fragment
hypotheses.hypothesis: Keep h3's dequant prepass and its plain raster, but change stage 2 to a 128x64x32 tile with the same 2x2 simdgroups (128 threads), so each simdgroup owns a 64x32 fragment (TM=8, TN=4) instead of 32x32. h7 widened the tile by adding simdgroups (8 SGs, about 15KB) and lost. This change keeps 4 SGs and raises MMA work per threadgroup-memory fragment load and per barrier, which targets the shared-memory and issue overhead in a GEMM that already runs near the bf16 flop rate. The per-output k order is unchanged, so the result stays bit-exact.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: whole-model speedup unresolved

hypotheses.hypothesis: Keep h3's dequant prepass and its 64x64x32 tile on 2x2 simdgroups. Change only how stage 2 feeds threadgroup memory. With 128 threads, each thread owns exactly one 16-element slice of the X slab and one of the W slab, so the code can be explicit. Each thread loads its slices for step k+1 into registers right after the second barrier, then issues the MMA for step k. At the top of the next iteration it copies those registers into threadgroup memory. Global-load latency then overlaps the MMA, and threadgroup memory stays at 10KB with no double buffer (lessons 39 and 44 suggest a bigger footprint hurts). Loads use 16-byte vectors. The k order per output is unchanged, so the result stays bit-exact. A fallback covers M not divisible by 64, K not divisible by 32, and batch above 1.
hypotheses.summary: shipped: whole-model correctness and independent timing confirmation passed

hypotheses.hypothesis: Keep the stage 2 that wins h9 or h3. Rewrite the dequant prepass so each thread dequantizes 32 values (4 words) under one scale and bias and writes them as 16-byte vectors. This cuts per-thread index math and narrow stores in the roughly 2ms stage. The values match the original bit for bit.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: whole-model speedup unresolved

hypotheses.kind: double-buffered tile, one barrier per step
hypotheses.hypothesis: Start from h9 and keep its dequant prepass, the 64x64x32 tile on 2x2 simdgroups, and the register prefetch. Add a second threadgroup buffer for X and for W and alternate between them each K step. The first barrier then goes away, leaving one barrier per step. Writing into buf[k&1] at step k is safe: that buffer was last read by the MMA of step k-2, and every thread finished that MMA before reaching the barrier of step k-1. Threadgroup memory grows from about 10KB to 20KB. The k order does not change, so the result stays bit-exact.
hypotheses.summary: correct_slower: slower than the installed kernel in a fresh region comparison; model timing skipped

hypotheses.hypothesis: If h11 loses, go back to h9 with BK=64, a single buffer and the register prefetch. Each thread prefetches 32 elements of X and 32 of W, which halves the barriers per flop. The k order is unchanged.
